newsitem.title: USA: Prince Charles pays New York City a 12-hour visit.
newsitem.headline: Prince Charles pays New York City a 12-hour visit.

text.p: Britain's Prince Charles made a 12-hour whirlwind visit to New York City on Tuesday where he visited the United Nations and was the guest of honour at a gala dinner at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

"I can't tell you what a pleasure it is for me to be here this evening at this marvellous gathering," he said in his brief remarks to some 300 founding sponsors of the American Associates of the St. Catherine Foundation.

"I feel perhaps like most of you, we've managed to walk a very long way to get here ... which has been a pilgrimage in itself ... to have come here by Concorde and now to wonder exactly what time of the day it is," he said, getting a ripple of laughter from the guests seated in the museum's "Temple of Dendur."
The foundation, which Charles helped create in London last year, raises funds for the preservation of art works at the Monastery of St. Catherine's at Mount Sinai in Egypt.

Charles was met at the museum by William Luers, president of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and Emily Rafferty, senior vice president for development at the museum. He was joined by former U.S. President George Bush, Princess Sumaya of Jordan, the daughter of King Hussein, and United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan.

From the moment Charles landed in New York shortly before 10 a.m. EST (1500 GMT) he was on the go, first meeting Annan, then lunching with a host of ambassadors including Britain's U.N. Ambassador John Weston, before attending a reception given by members of the Royal Shakespeare in the late afternoon.

The evening at the museum began with Charles and other guests touring the Greek and Roman gallery before entering the Great Hall where he, Bush and other dignitaries posed for pictures. The group then moved up the grand staircase to view "The Glory of Byzantium" exhibition.

The prince, who received a standing ovation before and after his remarks, said he was deeply moved by the exhibit and observed that many of the pieces on display had never before been exhibited publicly. He called the exhibit "remarkable" and "captivating."
